qs.q: A clinical officer is counseling a patient about long‑acting reversible contraception. Which method has a typical‑use failure rate of about 0.1–0.4 % per year?
qs.e: The levonorgestrel‑releasing intrauterine system is a LARC with a typical‑use failure of 0.1–0.4 % in the first year. The copper IUD has a slightly higher failure rate, and the other options are not LARC methods.

qs.q: A nursing student is asked to define contraception in clinical practice. Which statement is correct?
o: Use of assisted reproductive technologies to treat infertility in clinical practice.
Use of behavioral methods, medicines, devices, or procedures to prevent pregnancy.
Surgical tying or sealing of the fallopian tubes for permanent sterilization.
Natural fertilization and implantation processes that occur within the uterus.
qs.e: Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy using behavioral, pharmacologic, device, or procedural methods. The other options describe sterilization, the fertilization process, or infertility treatment, not contraception.

qs.q: A clinical team is discussing the advantages of Long-Acting Reversible Contraception over short-acting hormonal methods. What is a key characteristic of LARC methods?
o: Effectiveness relies completely on the user taking a daily action.
They show very low typical‑use failure since they work without per‑act use.
They offer guaranteed protection against every sexually transmitted infection.
They must be surgically removed each month.
qs.e: LARC methods have very low typical-use failure because they do not depend on daily or per-act action. They do not protect against STIs and do not require monthly removal.

qs.q: A 22‑year‑old postpartum woman, 4 weeks after vaginal delivery and exclusively breastfeeding, asks for contraception. Which method is most appropriate now?
qs.e: Copper IUCD can be inserted postpartum and is safe during breastfeeding, while combined hormones are contraindicated early postpartum. The LNG‑IUS is also delayed until at least 6 weeks postpartum for breastfeeding women.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

qs.q: A 31‑year‑old woman presents 48 hours after unprotected intercourse and wants emergency contraception. Which option provides the highest efficacy within this timeframe?
qs.e: Copper IUCD is the most effective emergency contraceptive up to 5 days after intercourse. Ulipristal is effective up to 5 days but slightly less than copper IUCD.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

qs.q: A 33‑year‑old woman with well‑controlled hypertension (BP 138/86 mmHg) asks about combined hormonal contraception. According to WHO MEC, what is the appropriate category for her?
qs.e: Mild to moderate hypertension places combined hormonal contraception in category 2, meaning it can be used with caution. Severe hypertension would be category 3 or 4.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

qs.q: A 22‑year‑old woman prefers a method that also offers protection against HIV. Which option best fulfills both contraception and STI protection?
qs.e: Male condoms provide both contraception and barrier protection against HIV and other STIs. Intrauterine devices and injectables do not protect against infections.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

qs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² seeks contraception. Which method is contraindicated due to increased VTE risk according to WHO MEC?
qs.e: Obesity (BMI ≥ 35) combined with estrogen‑containing pills raises VTE risk, placing them in category 3/4. Progestogen‑only and non‑hormonal methods remain acceptable.
qs.s: Contraception and Family Planning: Year 4: MCQs

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Contraception involves methods that prevent fertilisation or implantation. Clinicians must match patient goals, health status, and resource availability to choose safe, effective options.

sections.p: Contraception refers to any intentional method that prevents pregnancy. Diagnosis is clinical: confirming desire to avoid conception and assessing suitability of methods.
b: Identify reproductive intent
Assess contraindications (e.g., thrombosis, uncontrolled hypertension)

sections.p: Not a disease, but risk of unintended pregnancy can be staged by effectiveness: perfect-use failure rates (<1% for LARC) to typical-use (>20% for withdrawal).
b: High‑risk: no method or low‑effectiveness method
Moderate‑risk: pills, patches, rings
Low‑risk: IUDs, implants, sterilisation

sections.p: Failure of contraception is usually due to user error, method incompatibility, or drug interactions.
b: Incorrect use (missed pills, improper condom use)
Drug interactions reducing hormonal efficacy (rifampicin, antiepileptics)
Method failure (IUD expulsion, condom breakage)
Physiologic factors (obesity reducing hormonal levels)

sections.p: Patients present seeking advice, reporting breakthrough bleeding, or after an unintended pregnancy.
b: Desire for long‑acting reversible contraception (LARC)
Concern about side‑effects
Need for emergency contraception

sections.p: Testing ensures safety and informs method choice.
b: If labs unavailable, use clinical history (e.g., known hypertension) to guide safe method selection.

t.b: Is patient already pregnant? Positive result excludes hormonal methods and prompts abortion care or continuation counseling.
Is there hypertension? High BP contraindicates combined hormonal contraceptives.

t.a: CBC and liver function tests (if considering hormonal method)
t.b: Detect anemia, thrombophilia, or hepatic disease that may affect method safety.
Identify infections that influence choice of barrier methods and need for STI counseling.

sections.p: Complications are rare but can be serious.
b: IUD perforation or expulsion
Thromboembolic events with estrogen‑containing pills
Severe allergic reaction to device material

sections.p: Choose method based on effectiveness, contraindications, patient preference, and resource availability.
b: Long‑acting reversible contraception (copper IUD, hormonal IUD, implant) – highest efficacy, minimal user dependence.
Combined oral contraceptives – useful when estrogen not contraindicated; avoid in smokers >35, hypertension, migraine with aura.
Progestogen‑only pills/injectables – safe in hypertension, breastfeeding; watch for irregular bleeding.
Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragm) – add STI protection; use when hormonal methods unsuitable.
Emergency contraception – copper IUD up to 5 days; oral levonorgestrel up to 3 days if IUD unavailable.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate method tolerance, side‑effects, and reproductive goals at 3‑month intervals, then annually.
b: Check blood pressure after 1 month on combined pills
Inspect IUD strings at each visit
Provide counseling on STI prevention and dual‑method use

sections.p: Conditions that mimic contraceptive failure or side‑effects.
b: Polycystic ovary syndrome – irregular bleeding may be mistaken for hormonal method side‑effect
Pregnancy – must be ruled out before starting hormonal contraception
Menstrual disorders – breakthrough bleeding is common with progestogen‑only methods

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal.
b: Early pregnancy test may be negative if performed too soon; repeat in 48 h if suspicion remains
Blood pressure measured in a noisy environment may overestimate hypertension, leading to unnecessary avoidance of estrogen

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain after IUD insertion (possible perforation)
Sudden unilateral leg swelling or chest pain (possible thromboembolism)
Heavy vaginal bleeding not controlled with tampon or medication

faq.q: Can I use hormonal contraception while breastfeeding?
faq.a: Progestogen‑only methods are safe; combined estrogen‑containing pills are avoided until 6 weeks postpartum.

faq.q: Is the copper IUD safe for emergency contraception?
faq.a: Yes, it can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and provides ongoing contraception.

faq.q: What method is best for a woman with uncontrolled hypertension?
faq.a: Non‑estrogen options such as progestogen‑only pills, injectables, implants, or IUDs are preferred.
